stances.claim: True love of family is evidenced not by abstraction but by concrete extraordinary gifts: a brand-new Jaguar, a brand-new Bosendorfer piano, a custom pink-gumamela variety bred by UP Los Baños, and the Sylvia P. Lina Theater at De La Salle Zobel.

stances.claim: Genuine love of work means calling 2,800 employees 'partners and collaborators, not alalays,' providing them a free daily meal with healthy brown rice, and sharing production bonuses and profit-sharing regardless of rank — model labor practices grounded in dignity.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes an edited and abridged eulogy for his long-time friend Alberto 'Bert' David Lina, structured around Bert's three loves: family, work, and the Almighty God. Bert loved his wife Sylvia 'endearingly, tenderly, and eternally' -- she was 'the light of his life and the apple and mango of his eyes' -- and even in his 70s he was 'always Sylvia's swain of 20,' singing ballads, composing poems, and crafting love letters. Birthday gifts to Sylvia included a brand-new Jaguar car, a brand-new Bosendorfer piano, and a special pink-gumamela variety bred for her by UP Los Baños in her favorite color; he donated the auditorium at De La Salle Zobel in Alabang and christened it the Sylvia P. Lina Theater. He loved his four daughters (April Rose, Donna May, Sheila, Bertha Ann -- Valentine's roses, but no boyfriends until after college) and his four grandchildren (Andy, Alwyn, Aurelia Joule, Aurora Jane -- the only people who could countermand his orders). His second love was work: he loved to create, innovate, reinvent, and think out of the box, treating problems as opportunities; he loved all his 21 companies (some recently sold to the Ayala Group) across logistics, outsourcing, communications, connectivity, films, creative designs, sports, entertainment, land transportation, solar power, and waste management (the 'polite name of the portalet system he originated'); and he loved his 2,800 employees -- called 'partners and collaborators, not alalays' -- each getting a free daily meal with healthy brown rice, with production bonuses and profit-sharing regardless of rank. He loved the country 'warts and all' and twice took the tough job of customs commissioner against the author's advice -- once under Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, once under Benigno Aquino III. He also loved golf (hosting tournaments at company anniversaries and birthdays) and classical and popular music (indefatigable funder of the Manila Symphony Orchestra; logistics sponsor of the Philippine Philharmonic Orchestra and the Metro Manila Concert Orchestra). His third love was the Almighty: he credited the Lord with everything, framing himself as steward, and at the author's request donated ultramodern computerized Carillons at the Manila Cathedral, St. James Church in Alabang, Naga City, Pila Laguna, and Mandaue Cebu, telling the author that 'they reminded him of his mortality every time they chimed'; he loved the poor through medical-surgical-dental missions, annual company bloodletting, and support for the Red Cross and the little-known Guiding Light Ministries of Aklan. The author has known Bert since 1969 when he was a young L.C. Diaz and Company audit team member, was Bert and Sylvia's wedding sponsor, and considers Donna May his 'daughter by choice' (she calls him 'Dad CJ'). From those peso-and-centavo days, Bert -- 'the poor boy born in Tondo, Manila with roots in Laguna' -- rose to be a Filipino taipan in an authentic rags-to-riches story. The one word that unravels the secret of his gargantuan success was LOVE -- 'his enormous, googolplex love for his family, for his work, and for our Almighty Lord. Truly, to God be the glory!'
